points.text: Byte pair encoding is the tokenizer used behind modern large language models such as GPT-2, GPT-3, and the original model used in ChatGPT, so it is important to understand it.
In the previous lecture, the tokenizer converted sentences into tokens, arranged the tokens into a vocabulary in ascending order, and assigned each token a numerical token ID.
In the simple tokenizer from the previous lecture, every word was treated as a unique token, along with special characters such as commas, full stops, and exclamation marks.
There are three types of tokenization algorithms: word-based tokenizers, subword-based tokenizers, and character-based tokenizers.
In a word-based tokenizer, each word in a sentence is usually one token.
If the sentence is "my hobby is playing cricket" and the tokens are the individual words "my," "hobby," "is," "playing," and "cricket," then that is a word-based tokenizer.
A main problem with word-based tokenization is handling words that are not present in the vocabulary, which are called out-of-vocabulary words.
Out-of-vocabulary words in word-based tokenization are like preparing for an exam and being asked a completely different question in the exam.
If a user inputs a word that is not in the vocabulary, a word-based tokenization scheme can run into an error.
A vocabulary is a dictionary containing a collection of tokens arranged in ascending order, and each token corresponds to a token ID.
Word-based tokenization does not capture similarity between related words such as "boy" and "boys," because they are treated as separate words.
In character-based tokenization, individual characters are considered tokens instead of whole words.
For the sentence "my hobby is playing cricket," character-based tokenization would use characters such as m, y, h, o, and b as tokens instead of individual words.
Character-based tokenization leads to a very small vocabulary because every language has a fixed number of characters.
In the English language, the lecturer states that there are 256 characters, while there are about 170,000 to 200,000 words.
An advantage of character-based tokenization is that it avoids the out-of-vocabulary problem, because any new sentence can always be broken into characters that are already in the vocabulary.
Character-based tokenization also solves the problem of large vocabulary size in word-based tokenization because its vocabulary is based on characters and is therefore small.
Character-based tokenization is computationally and memory efficient because the vocabulary size is very small.
A major problem with character-based tokenization is that the meaning associated with words is completely lost when text is broken into individual characters.
Another problem with character-based tokenization is that the tokenized sequence is much longer than the initial raw text.
For example, the word "dinosaur" is one token in word-based tokenization but becomes eight separate character tokens in character-based tokenization.
Word-based tokenization produces shorter tokenized sequences because each word is one token, but its disadvantages are out-of-vocabulary words and a large vocabulary size.
Character-based tokenization has a small fixed vocabulary and avoids out-of-vocabulary words, but it produces tokenized sequences that are much longer than the original text.
Both word-based and character-based tokenization fail to capture common roots or shared parts such as the root in "boy" and "boys" or the shared "isation" in related words.
Subword-based tokenization is another tokenization algorithm, and byte pair encoding is an example of a subword-based tokenization algorithm.
Subword-based tokenization is presented as a best-of-both-worlds approach between word tokenization and character tokenization.
Subword-based tokenization captures some root words that occur in many other words, such as treating "boy" as the common root in related words.
The first rule of subword-based tokenization is that frequently used words in the dataset should not be split into smaller subwords.
The second rule of subword-based tokenization is that rare words should be split into smaller meaningful subwords, and this can go down to the character level if needed.
Subword-based tokenization combines features of word tokenization and character tokenization because frequent words are kept whole while rare words can be broken down further.
For example, if "boy" appears multiple times in the dataset, it is kept as a token, but "boys" can be split into the meaningful subwords "boy" and "s."
The main essence of subword tokenization is that words are sometimes broken into smaller elements because those smaller elements appear very frequently.
An advantage of subword tokenization is that subword splitting helps the model learn that words such as "token," "tokens," and "tokenizing" share the same root word and are similar in meaning.
Subword tokenization helps the model learn that words like tokenization and modernization share a common suffix even though they have different roots.
In subword tokenization, a word like tokenization can be broken into subword pieces such as a suffix token and root-related tokens, which helps the model learn common patterns across words.
Breaking one word into subwords has important advantages, and this is what is mainly done in subword tokenization.
Byte pair encoding, or BPE, is a subword tokenization algorithm.
Modern LLMs like GPT-2 and GPT-3 employ byte pair encoding.
The byte pair algorithm was introduced in 1994 as a data compression algorithm.
In byte pair encoding for compression, you scan the data, find the most common pair of consecutive bytes, replace it with a byte that does not occur in the data, and repeat this iteratively.
The lecturer shows the 1994 paper that introduced the byte pair algorithm for data compression.
In the example sequence, the most common byte pair is AA, not AAA, because byte pairs contain only two consecutive symbols.
In the example, the most frequent pair AA is replaced with Z because Z does not occur in the data, producing a shorter sequence.
After the first replacement, the process repeats by finding the next most frequent pair, and in the example AB is replaced with Y because Y does not occur in the data.
Replacing common byte pairs with another symbol is called encoding, which is why the method is called an encoder.
The compression process stops when no byte pair occurs more than once, although the example can be compressed one layer further by replacing ZY with another symbol.
The byte pair encoding algorithm scans the data, identifies the most frequent byte pairs, replaces them with a byte not present in the data, and repeats until no byte pair appears more than once.
For large language models, byte pair encoding is slightly modified so that it converts sentences into subwords.
For LLMs, byte pair encoding aims to represent the most common words as single tokens and to break rare words into two or more subword tokens.
The dataset of words used in the example is also called a data corpus.
In the example corpus, word-based tokenization would treat old, older, finest, and lowest as four tokens, while character-level tokenization would treat each character as a token.
Before applying BPE to words for subword tokenization, a preprocessing step appends an end-of-word token to each word so the tokenizer knows where the word ends.
In the example, each word is augmented with the end-of-word marker, so old, older, finest, and lowest are all written with an added end token.
Word-based and character-based tokenization do not capture shared roots or meaningful subword structure such as the relationship between old and older or the shared ending in finest and lowest.
The first step in the subword BPE example is to split the words into characters and make a frequency table using the word frequencies in the corpus.
Because every word in the example corpus has the end-of-word marker, that marker appears once for every word token in the corpus.
At the character level in the example, there are 12 tokens, and character-level tokenization would stop there because each character would remain an individual token.
In the modified BPE used for subword tokenization, you repeatedly find the most frequent pairing in the dataset and merge that pair instead of replacing it with a new byte outside the data.
In the first iteration of the word example, the most frequent pairing is E and S, which occurs 13 times across finest and lowest.
After finding that E and S is the most frequent pair, the tokenizer merges them into a single subword token ES and updates the token table accordingly.
When ES is added as a token, its count is subtracted from the counts of E and S, and in this example S never appears without E.
Once ES becomes a token, EST becomes a new byte pair made of ES and T, and it is the most frequent pair in the next iteration.
In byte pair encoding, you repeatedly merge the byte pair that appears most often in the dataset into a new token.
In this example, the pair "es" appears most, so a token for "es" is created first, and then the pair "es" and "t" is merged into the token "EST" because it occurs 13 times.
After creating the token "EST", its count becomes 13 and the previous token "es" drops to zero occurrences in this example.
Byte pair encoding can identify "EST" as a common root between words like "finest" and "lowest", which word-level and character-level tokenizers could not capture.
In the next iteration, "EST" and the end-of-word marker are merged because that pair appears 13 times and more often than any other byte pair in the words.

Merging "EST" with the end-of-word marker encodes that "EST" is an ending sequence in the dataset, allowing the tokenizer to distinguish a word like "highest" from a word like "estimate" where "EST" is not at the end.
Once the final merged token with the end-of-word marker is created, the intermediate tokens "es" and "EST" are no longer needed.
The pair "o" and "l" occurs 10 times in this example, so it is merged into a new token, and then that token is merged with "d" to form the token "old".
The tokens produced by byte pair encoding are subwords rather than full words or single characters, and they can encode root representations.
The token "old" captures a root that appears in both "old" and "older", showing that byte pair encoding can capture root words that word-level and character-level tokenizers miss.

A frequent sequence that appears only within one word, such as the sequence in "finest", should not necessarily be merged into a token, because subword tokens are useful when they recur across multiple words.
A rule of subword tokenization is that a word part that occurs multiple times can be kept as its own token, while less reusable words are split into reusable subwords and characters.
After constructing merged tokens, you can remove tokens whose frequency has become zero to obtain the final token table.
The final tokens from the subword tokenizer are used as the vocabulary for later large language model training steps such as vector embedding.
Byte pair encoding is a subword tokenizer used for training models like GPT-2 and GPT-3.
It is called a subword tokenizer because its vocabulary contains units like "EST" that are neither full words nor single characters but subwords.
Byte pair encoding stops merging based on a specified stopping criterion, such as reaching a target token count or a chosen number of iterations.
Compared with word-level encoding, byte pair encoding can reduce the number of tokens because related words like "boy" and "boys" do not both need to be separate full-word tokens.
The lecturer states that GPT-2 or GPT-3 used roughly 50,000 to 57,000 tokens after byte pair encoding.
Byte pair encoding helps solve the out-of-vocabulary problem because its vocabulary includes subwords and sometimes characters.
Subword encoding keeps the advantages of character-level tokenization while also capturing root meanings and avoiding the very large vocabulary of word-level encoding.
Implementing byte pair encoding from scratch is relatively complicated, so the lecturer uses the Python open-source library tiktoken, which is used by OpenAI models.
To use tiktoken, you first install it, then instantiate the GPT-2 byte pair encoding tokenizer with a call like get_encoding("gpt2").
The tokenizer object from tiktoken is similar to the earlier tokenizer classes defined in Python, but it is created in one line through the library.
A tokenizer has an encode method that converts words into token IDs and a decode method that converts token IDs back into words.
The end-of-text token is used to mark that one text has ended and another has started, and it is part of the GPT-2 vocabulary.
A rare or unknown word can cause an out-of-vocabulary problem for a word-level tokenizer, but a byte pair encoder can still encode it using characters and subwords.
The example code encodes a sentence into token IDs, including the end-of-text token with ID 50256.
In the GPT-2 and GPT-3 tokenization scheme, token ID 50256 is the end-of-text token.
The GPT-2 and GPT-3 byte pair encoding tokenizer uses a vocabulary of about 50,000 tokens, which is much smaller than a word-level English vocabulary of roughly 170,000 to 200,000 words.
Byte pair encoding reduces vocabulary size while still giving strong model performance.
Subword tokenization can handle out-of-vocabulary text by breaking unknown words into several subwords.
A tokenizer provides both an encode method to convert text into token IDs and a decode method to convert token IDs back into text.
The code uses the decode method on the token IDs and reconstructs the same sentence that was originally given to the tokenizer.
The lecturer highlights two advantages of byte pair encoding: it reduces vocabulary size and it can deal with unknown text.
In the GPT-2 byte pair tokenizer, the end-of-text token is the last token in the vocabulary and has the largest token ID, 50256.
The byte pair tokenizer used for GPT-2, GPT-3, and the original model used in ChatGPT has a total vocabulary size of 50257.
A byte pair encoding tokenizer can correctly encode and decode unknown words without needing a special unknown-word token because it works at the level of characters and subwords.
The algorithm underlying byte pair encoding breaks words that are not in its predefined vocabulary into smaller subword units or even individual characters.
Because byte pair encoding can represent an unfamiliar word as a sequence of subword tokens or characters, it can handle out-of-vocabulary words.
When random nonsense words are passed to the tiktoken GPT-2 byte pair encoder, it does not raise an error and instead encodes them into tokens.
For an unknown word, the tokenizer breaks the text into subwords or characters based on what exists in the vocabulary and assigns each piece a token ID.
To encode unknown text, the tokenizer scans from left to right, breaks the text into characters or subwords, and assigns each character or subword a token ID.
Decoding the resulting integers gives back exactly the same sentence that was originally encoded.
The lecture taught what byte pair encoding is, how to install tiktoken and use the GPT-2 byte pair tokenizer, how it handles unknown words, and that its vocabulary size is about 50,000.

A schematic is shown to illustrate that the course has covered tokenizing input text into token IDs, including a custom tokenizer in the previous lecture and byte pair encoding in this lecture, and has not yet covered token embeddings.
The lecture also covered intuitive whiteboard iterations of the byte pair encoder and coding a byte pair encoder in Python using the tiktoken library.
